1a:
**Grading note for sub-item 1a**

Grade this item on substance, not wording: the rubric is pointing at the aliasing relationship between `result` and `reply.result`, so credit any answer that correctly connects the `deepcopy(result)` to whether the serialization of `result[DATA]` shows up in `reply.result[DATA]`. Do not require the literal rubric phrasing or any particular direction of the counterfactual. An answer earns the point if it asserts the shared-reference mechanism — that `result` and `reply.result` are the same object, so mutating or serializing `result[DATA]` would also change `reply.result[DATA]` unless a deepcopy is taken — and it equally earns the point with the technically accurate inverse phrasing ("without the deepcopy, the serialization would propagate into `reply.result[DATA]`"). A positive, non-counterfactual formulation is just as acceptable: saying that the deepcopy makes `result` an independent copy so that serializing `result[DATA]` leaves `reply.result[DATA]` untouched conveys the same fact and earns credit. Hedging or conditioning does not cost the point either, so long as the identity/propagation fact is affirmatively stated — e.g. framing it as "copy it if the original is needed later" still counts, provided the answer names the shared reference or the resulting (non-)propagation.

Deduct the 1 point only when the answer never connects the `deepcopy` to the relationship (or non-relationship) between the serialized `result[DATA]` and `reply.result[DATA]` at all — for example, vague "maybe copy for consistency / safety" advice that never names the aliasing or the propagation of the serialization.
1b: Apply this sub-item only to penalize discussion of transaction types that fall genuinely outside the SCHEMA/ISSUER_KEY scope. Deduct the 2 points when the answer brings in and discusses the deepcopy's implications for unrelated transaction types such as NYM or ATTRIB. Do not deduct when the answer's references stay within the SCHEMA/ISSUER_KEY concept space — this includes types that are the same concept under a different or later name (e.g., CLAIM_DEF as the successor to ISSUER_KEY) and the read counterparts of the two in-scope types (e.g., GET_SCHEMA for SCHEMA); treat all of these as in-scope rather than as "other" transaction types. Likewise, an answer that discusses only SCHEMA and ISSUER_KEY receives no deduction.
2a:
**Sub-item 2a (1 point) — the serialized data being reflected in the ledger.**

Award the point (no_deduct) when the answer states, as a matter of fact, that the deepcopy is required and explains why — i.e. that after the `deepcopy(result)` the serialized `result[DATA]` is what goes on to be written to / reflected in the ledger — and makes that claim flatly, without an escape clause that would turn the deepcopy into an optional step. A straight assertion plus the reason is enough; the grader should not demand any further qualification once the ledger consequence is stated outright.

Deduct the point when the answer never mentions that the data serialization is reflected in the ledger at all, or when it only raises the point conditionally or hedged — e.g. framing it as "if you need the serialized form later…", "this might be reflected in the ledger", or "if you don't need it, the deepcopy isn't required" — since such phrasing makes the need conditional rather than committing to it. Hedged or conditional treatment is scored the same as not mentioning it.
2b:
**Grading note for sub-item 2b (data serialization is not reflected in the graph):**

Award no deduction only when the answer makes clear — by explicit statement or by direct implication — that the serialized form of `result[DATA]` does not reach the graph, and does so with enough explanation to count as discussion rather than a passing remark.

Three things must hold together. First, the **graph must be named**: the answer has to identify the graph store specifically as the destination that keeps the unmodified data — wording such as "the graph," "graph storage," "the OrientDB graph," or "`storeTxnInGraph`" all qualify. Generic references to "other consumers," "the client/reply," "the in-memory copy," or "downstream code," with no mention of the graph, do not satisfy this and earn the deduction. Second, the **direction of data flow must be correct**: the serialized copy goes to the ledger write, while the graph (or other post-deepcopy storage/field-additions path) receives the unmodified dict. If the answer reverses this — treating the ledger as the consumer that needs the pristine original — deduct. Third, the point must be **discussed, not merely dropped in**: the answer must state (or clearly imply) the fact and tie it to why or how it arises — the `deepcopy` at that call site — or to what it means for what the graph ends up storing. A single-line drive-by assertion with no explanation counts as not discussed and earns the deduction.

The exact words "serialization is not reflected in the graph" are not required. Formulations from which the fact directly follows are sufficient, e.g. "`deepcopy` keeps the original `result` intact so the graph gets the unmodified dict," or "`reply.result` still holds the dict form when it is stored in the graph." Deduct only when neither the statement nor a direct implication of it is present, when the graph is never named as the non-receiving destination, when the ledger/graph roles are reversed, or when the point appears only as an unexplained one-liner.
